source_refs.note: Topic 2.5.1, printed pages 29-30: the principal quantum number and the 2n squared rule.

blocks.text: The principal quantum number n can have the positive integral values 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on, designated K, L, M, N, and corresponds to the orbit number of Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom. It describes the size and energy of the orbital. The collection of orbitals with the same value of n is an electron shell. The larger n, the greater the average distance of an electron in the orbital from the nucleus and so the larger the orbital; a higher n also means the electron has higher energy and is less tightly bound to the nucleus. The principal quantum number also gives the maximum number of electrons in a shell by the formula 2n squared, so the K, L, M and N shells can hold 2, 8, 18 and 32 electrons respectively.

blocks.prompt: An electron has n = 3. What can you say about its shell, its distance from the nucleus and how tightly it is held, compared with an electron of n = 1?
blocks.explanation: It is in the M shell, which can hold up to 18 electrons. On average it is farther from the nucleus than an n = 1 electron, so its orbital is larger, its energy is higher and it is less tightly bound.

items: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 (K, L, M, N): size and energy of the orbital; larger n means a larger, higher-energy, less tightly bound orbital. A shell holds at most 2n squared electrons: 2, 8, 18, 32.
